title: Is BERT Really Robust? A Strong Baseline for Natural Language Attack on Text Classification and Entailment
authors: Di Jin, Zhijing Jin, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Peter Szolovits

blocks.html: Adversarial examples are easy to picture for images — add invisible pixel noise. Text is harder: words are discrete, so you cannot nudge them by a tiny amount, and any change a human can read. The challenge is to alter a sentence enough to flip a classifier while a person still sees the same meaning, fluent grammar, and the same correct label.

TextFooler is a black-box attack that does exactly this for modern text models including BERT. It does not need the model's weights or gradients — only the ability to query it and read the output probabilities.

The recipe: (1) find the few words that matter most to the prediction, then (2) replace them with meaning-preserving synonyms until the label flips while staying grammatical and semantically faithful.

Changing every word would wreck the sentence. TextFooler first asks: which words actually drive the model's decision? It deletes each word in turn and measures how much the model's confidence in the correct label drops. A big drop means that word was important.

Read this as: the importance $I_{w_i}$ of word $w_i$ is the model's probability for the true label $y$ on the full sentence $X$ minus its probability after removing that word ($X_{\setminus w_i}$). The larger this gap, the more the model leans on $w_i$.

Words are then sorted by importance, and the attack targets the top ones first. This keeps the attack efficient — changing a handful of high-impact words is usually enough, which also keeps the sentence close to the original.
For each important word, TextFooler gathers candidate replacements and filters them through several constraints so the swap stays invisible to a human reader:

items: Synonym extraction: take the nearest neighbors of the word in a counter-fitted word-embedding space. Counter-fitting reshapes embeddings so that genuine synonyms are close and antonyms are pushed apart — avoiding the classic trap where 'good' and 'bad' look similar.
Part-of-speech match: keep only candidates with the same POS (replace a verb with a verb, a noun with a noun) so grammar is preserved.
Semantic similarity check: embed the original and candidate sentences with a Universal Sentence Encoder and keep the swap only if overall sentence meaning stays above a similarity threshold.

blocks.html: Among the survivors, the attacker picks the replacement that most reduces the model's confidence in the correct label (or pushes it toward the target label). If a single swap already flips the prediction, the attack stops; otherwise it moves to the next important word and repeats.

In words: only accept a candidate $c$ if the adversarial sentence stays within a sentence-similarity threshold $\tau$ of the original and the candidate shares the word's part of speech. These two guards are what keep the result fluent and meaning-preserving.

TextFooler is a greedy procedure. It walks down the importance-ranked word list and, for each word, makes the best meaning-preserving swap it can, checking after every change whether the label has flipped.

items: For the most important remaining word, build the filtered synonym candidate set (Step 2).
Choose the candidate that most hurts the true-label confidence while passing the POS and similarity constraints.
If the prediction has flipped, return the adversarial sentence; otherwise keep this swap and move to the next word.
Stop when the label flips or the candidates run out.

blocks.html: Because it is purely query-based, the attack works on any text classifier behind an API. It needs no gradients, which makes it a realistic black-box threat and a strong, reusable baseline for measuring NLP robustness.

Across classification and textual-entailment benchmarks, TextFooler drives the accuracy of strong models — including BERT, WordCNN, and LSTM classifiers — down to a small fraction of the original, often near or below 10-20%, while changing only a small percentage of the words in each sentence.

Critically, the perturbations are cheap and stealthy: a handful of synonym swaps per sentence. The answer to the title's question — 'Is BERT really robust?' — is a clear no against meaning-preserving word substitutions.

blocks.html: An attack on text is only valid if humans still read the adversarial sentence as the same content with the same label. The authors run human studies on grammaticality, meaning preservation, and human label agreement, and find the perturbed sentences largely retain their original meaning and human-assigned label.

The threat is genuine: the model is fooled, but a human is not. That gap — exactly the opposite of a typo or gibberish attack — is what makes synonym substitution a meaningful adversarial example for NLP.

TextFooler became a standard baseline and stress test for NLP robustness, motivating defenses such as adversarial training with synonym sets, certified word-substitution robustness, and more careful evaluation of just how brittle large language models are to word-level changes that humans barely notice.
